[TODAY] 1.5 billion Suns, when the universe was young. 🌌

Using the James Webb Space Telescope and Gemini North in Hawaii, astronomers found two quasars, feeding black holes that outshine their galaxies, just 18,100 light-years apart. We see them as they were 900 million years after the Big Bang. It is the oldest compact quasar pair known.

The bigger black hole weighs about 1.5 billion Suns, the smaller about 400 million. The team says no theory fully explains how they grew so big so early.

Reality check: a model is still needed to rule out a lens effect creating a double image.

How did they grow so fast? Share your guess below.

[TODAY] Hubble has no engine to stay up. 🔭

Like every spacecraft in low Earth orbit, the Hubble Space Telescope is slowly sinking as thin air drags on it. It has no propulsion system to climb back. NASA expects it to reenter the atmosphere around 2033 to 2034, so a rescue would need to fly by 2032.

On Oct. 29, NASA asked companies how they could boost Hubble higher, upgrade it or guide it down safely at the end. Answers are due Nov. 30.

Reality check: this is a request for information, not a mission. Hubble is still working and making discoveries after more than 35 years.

Boost Hubble or let it retire? Tell us below.

[TODAY] Why do you never see the Moon's back? 🌕

The Moon does spin. But one turn on its axis takes exactly as long as one trip around Earth, so the same face always points at us. Astronomers call it tidal locking.

It started early. Earth's gravity stretched the young, molten Moon into a slight bulge that kept lagging behind its spin. That tug of war turned spin energy into heat until the rotation matched the orbit.

Reality check: it's not unusual. All the solar system's large moons are locked to their planets. Our Moon is also drifting away by about 4 cm (1.5 inches) a year.

Save this for the next full Moon you see.

[TODAY] Europa's sodium cloud has stayed steady since 1999. 🪐

Jupiter's moon Europa hides an ocean under its ice. Around it floats a faint cloud of sodium, part of table salt, reaching as far as 30 times Europa's radius. Using Keck Observatory data going back to 1999, a Boston University-led team found the cloud has barely changed.

That matters because the volcanic moon Io sprays sodium all over Jupiter's neighborhood. The cloud ignored Io's activity, so the team concludes it comes from Europa's own saltwater.

Reality check: this is an indirect clue, not a sample of the ocean. Next, they are using Hubble to look for magnesium.

What should we look for next on Europa? Tell us below.

[IMAGINE] Moon nights last about two weeks. 🌑

What is real: on Nov. 23, NASA asked companies to design and test Lunar Reactor-1, a small fission power system for the Moon. It should deliver 20 kilowatts, about what 16 average U.S. homes use, be launch-ready by 2030 and run for at least five years. Unlike solar panels, a reactor keeps working through the long lunar night.

Reality check: this is a call for proposals, due Dec. 21. Nothing is built or contracted yet. It must meet U.S. nuclear safety standards.

The speculation: what if Moon bases never had to ration power through the dark?

Fission on the Moon: smart or risky? Tell us below.
